edges.effect_quant: The strongest evidence shows a graded inverse association between lactation duration and maternal type 2 diabetes risk. This pattern appears in pooled observational evidence and in well-characterized long-term cohorts that measured diabetes biochemically rather than relying only on self-report.
edges.population: parous women followed postpartum into later adult life
edges.mechanism: Lactation increases glucose utilization and improves insulin sensitivity during the postpartum period, which may help reverse pregnancy-related metabolic stress. Women who breastfeed longer also show more favorable trajectories in glucose handling after gestational diabetes and across later childbearing years.
edges.summary: Longer breastfeeding duration is associated with lower later maternal type 2 diabetes risk. The association is dose-responsive in meta-analysis and remains visible in strong long-term cohort studies, making this one of the more credible maternal health benefits linked to lactation duration.
edges.caveats: This is still observational evidence, so confounding by baseline health and postpartum behaviors cannot be eliminated. The protective signal is strongest over longer follow-up and may be particularly pronounced in women with gestational diabetes, but not every short-term postpartum study shows the same magnitude.

evidence.citation: PinhoGomesAC et al 2021 Diabetes Obes Metab
evidence.notes: Association of lactation with maternal risk of type 2 diabetes: A systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies.
